Tu. śalya, śallè, sēlè, cēlè a thin upper cloth, generally without border. Te. sellä a cloth without a border; cēla, cēlamu cloth, clothing. Skt. cela clothes, garment. Mar. sela a sort of robe. Cf. rows.etymology: 1312. The following lemma is widespread in the Outer Languages but has been occasionally borrowed into Inner Languages; the fact that the lemma is not found in Turner sup- ports this assumption: Bng. rɔgṇɔ ‘to behave like a hero’, rɔgɔ n.m. ‘hero, combatant’, rɔgɔnt ‘heroic, combative’, rɔgi ‘heroic’, rɔgmɔgɔ ‘becoming more heroic’, rɔgmɔ̃ ‘more or very heroic’, ragiṇɔ ‘to be hostile, to fight’ and rāg n.m. ‘enmity, hostility’ are per- haps part of a series of contamination, cf. Ku. rag ‘enmity’ and ragragān ‘enraged’, P. rag ‘anger, passion’ — M.nāg. rāg ‘rage’, G. rāg ‘anger’ (LSI [ix ,ii: 456]), S. raɠiḍāī ‘quarrelsome, litigious; a wrangler’, Mult. kurāg ‘a cow neither yielding milk nor in calf’ (O’Brien [1881: 29]), Bhil. rig ‘anger’, Ahīrī dialect of Bhil. ragavāyō ‘got angry’, Bhil. poet. ragro ‘fight’ and ragrāvlũ ‘royal palace’ which is a compound with second component < OIA rājakula- ‘palace’ (10676), Ko. and M. rāg ‘anger’, rāgābărit ‘furi- ous’ (with OIA bharita- ‘filled with’), rāgiṣṭ ‘angry’; Ko.kuṇ. rag ‘wrath’ and ragav ‘to get angry’, PKT ragɔ ‘anger’, B. rāg ‘anger’, B.chit. and B.roh. rak ‘anger’ and raɣɔn ‘to get angry’, Or. rāgɔ ‘anger’ (also borrowed into Kh. ragom ‘become angry’ and Mu. rakṭāo ‘to be mad with rage’). All are related with OIA (TA) rágha- probably ‘anger, evil; Ärger, Böses’ (EWA). Since there is also the semantically rather inverse Bng. rɔgɔ ‘bad, nasty; fellow who is. . . ’, rɔgɔnt ‘hostile; bad, nasty’ there may be contamination with OIA rakta- ‘impassioned’ (10584) where Turner quotes Ku. rāgo ‘hatred’ (but voicing is implausible) etc., which in turn even suggests contamination (in case of the quoted H. word ragnā ‘to be in love with’) with OIA rāga- ‘passion, love’ (10674). Notes: (a) Related with the second Bng. meaning rɔgɔ ‘bad, nasty; fellow who is. . . ’ seem to be Kal. riganyók and righuí both ‘afraid, scared, timid’. (b) Bomhard (1995: 42 and CINCL 951) suggests a PN lemma *rag-/*rəg- ‘to stir, move, shake’ and he quotes Mann (1984-87: 1085) who reconstructs PIE *roghos ‘dashing, swift, bold’ with reflexes like Old Irish ráig ‘outburst’ (and reflexes in Proto-Afroasiatic).
